subject: science
passage: Appointed in 1904 to head India's meteorological observatories, the British mathematician Gilbert Walker was given a practical task: forecasting the strength of the summer monsoon, on which harvests across the subcontinent depended. Lacking an adequate physical theory of the monsoon, he searched instead for statistical correlations, comparing records of air pressure, temperature, and rainfall from stations around the world. Among the patterns he identified was a seesaw in air pressure between the Pacific and Indian Ocean regions, which he named the Southern Oscillation. His forecasts proved only modestly successful, and some contemporaries regarded correlations without a known cause as of doubtful value. Not until the 1960s did researchers show that the oscillation is coupled to periodic warming of the eastern Pacific, the phenomenon known as El Niño.
stem: Based on the text, why did Walker rely on statistical correlations in his work?

choices.A: Records from stations around the world were the only data that his observatories had.
choices.B: Harvests across the subcontinent depended on the strength of the summer monsoon.
choices.C: He had already shown that the Southern Oscillation was linked to El Niño.
choices.D: No adequate physical theory of the monsoon existed on which to base his forecasts.

explanation.why: The second sentence gives the reason: "Lacking an adequate physical theory of the monsoon, he searched instead for statistical correlations." The word "instead" shows that correlations were a substitute for the theory he did not have.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says what other data the observatories held; it says he compared records from around the world.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why forecasting the monsoon mattered, not why Walker used correlations to do it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The link to El Niño was shown "not until the 1960s," by later researchers.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the reason in the second sentence: correlations took the place of a missing physical theory.
